title: Count Valid Paths in a Tree
statement:
An undirected tree has `n` nodes numbered `1` to `n`, and `edges` lists its `n - 1` edges, each as `[u, v]`. Between any two different nodes `a` and `b` there is exactly one simple path; call it valid when exactly one of the node numbers on it (endpoints included) is a prime number.

Return how many unordered pairs of different nodes `{a, b}` have a valid path. The pair `{a, b}` is the same as `{b, a}` and counts once. The answer can exceed the 32-bit range, so the result is a 64-bit integer.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every pair of nodes and walking the path between them is O(n²) or worse. Flip the view: a valid path contains exactly one prime, so group paths by that prime. If you delete every prime node, the remaining non-prime nodes fall apart into connected pieces. A valid path through prime `p` either starts at `p` and ends inside one non-prime piece touching `p`, or runs from one such piece, through `p`, into a different piece. So all that matters is the size of each non-prime piece, which a flood fill finds once.

## Approach

1. Sieve `isPrime` for `0..n` and build the adjacency list `graph`.
2. `fill(start)` runs an iterative DFS over non-prime nodes only, collects the piece in `component`, and stores its length in `size` for every node of the piece (`0` means not visited yet, `-1` means on the stack).
3. For each `prime`, walk its non-prime neighbours `next`. Fill the piece if needed.
4. That piece adds `size[next]` paths ending at `prime`, plus `size[next] * reached` paths to the pieces already seen around this prime. Both together are `size[next] * (reached + 1)`. Then add `size[next]` to `reached`.
5. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

Primes are `2, 3, 5`. The non-prime pieces are `{1}` and `{4}`. Prime `2` has non-prime neighbours `1` and `4`: the first adds `1 * (0 + 1) = 1` (path 2–1), the second adds `1 * (1 + 1) = 2` (paths 2–4 and 1–4). Prime `3` touches piece `{1}` and adds `1`. Prime `5` touches only `2`, a prime, and adds nothing. `total = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log log n) for the sieve plus O(n) for the graph, the fills and the prime loop.
- Space: O(n) for `isPrime`, `graph` and `size`.

## Pitfalls

- `1` is not prime, so it belongs to the non-prime pieces.
- Each piece is filled once and its size reused; refilling it for every adjacent prime can be O(n²) on a star.
- Two non-prime neighbours of the same prime are always in different pieces (a tree has no cycles), so the products never double count.
- Use an explicit stack: a recursive DFS can overflow on a long chain of non-prime nodes.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `isPrime` | sieve result for every label |
| `graph` | adjacency list of the tree |
| `size` | size of the non-prime piece a node belongs to (`0` = unseen) |
| `fill` | flood fill that measures one non-prime piece |
| `reached` | non-prime nodes already met around the current prime |
| `total` | number of valid paths so far |

narration.2: Start a sieve: assume every label is prime.
narration.3: Node 0 does not exist and 1 is not prime.
narration.5: Sieve of Eratosthenes up to n.
narration.7: Cross out every multiple of the prime p, starting at p * p.
narration.11: Build an adjacency list for the tree.
narration.16: size will hold, for each non-prime node, how many nodes are in its non-prime piece.
narration.17: Flood fill one connected piece of non-prime nodes with an explicit DFS stack.
narration.21: Keep exploring until the stack is empty.
narration.25: Only step into non-prime nodes that have not been visited yet.
narration.32: Every node of the piece learns the piece's size.
narration.36: Count valid paths by the single prime they contain.
narration.39: Look at each neighbour of this prime.
narration.40: A prime neighbour would put two primes on the path, so skip it.
narration.41: Measure this neighbour's non-prime piece the first time it is met.
narration.42: Paths from the prime into this piece, plus paths joining this piece to earlier pieces through the prime.
narration.43: These nodes are now available to pair with later pieces around the same prime.
narration.46: Every valid path was counted exactly once, at its only prime.
